title: The whirlwind
hook: God answers with stars, sea and wild animals, not with a reason (Job 38–39)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Job argues: he asks for a hearing, and the book lets his complaint stand. Today he gets his hearing, though not the one he asked for.

What would you say if you finally got the meeting? Job has had chapter after chapter to prepare. He has his case and his arguments, and he has waited. Then, after all the talking, the voice he's been asking for arrives, and not quietly. "Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind." What comes back from the storm is a long list of questions of its own.
screen: `JOB HAS HIS CASE READY.` → `THE VOICE ARRIVES.` → `OUT OF THE WHIRLWIND.`

segments.voice: First, questions for questions. The very first thing God asks: "Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? declare, if thou hast understanding." Not an accusation of sin; a question about scale. Second, stars and sea. The questions keep coming, and they're beautiful. Where was Job when the earth's cornerstone was laid, "When the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy?" Who shut in the sea and told it: "Hitherto shalt thou come, but no further: and here shall thy proud waves be stayed"? Can you bind the Pleiades, or loosen the bands of Orion? Third, animals nobody tamed. The wild donkey who laughs at the noise of the city. The wild ox who won't be harnessed. The ostrich. The war horse: "hast thou clothed his neck with thunder?" The hawk: "Doth the hawk fly by thy wisdom, and stretch her wings toward the south?" A whole world going about its business with no human in charge of it. Fourth, no reason, and still an answer. God never mentions the scene in heaven from chapter one. Job is never told why. And yet his reply, near the end, is this: "I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear: but now mine eye seeth thee." Readers have heard the whirlwind in different ways. Some hear a rebuke, putting Job in his place. Some hear comfort, that the world is held by someone bigger than the question. Some hear an invitation out of the ash heap and into a much wider world. The book doesn't settle it. It answers the argument by showing Job the world.
screen: `QUESTIONS FOR QUESTIONS.` · `STARS SING, THE SEA STOPS.` · `ANIMALS NOBODY TAMED.` · `NO REASON, AND STILL AN ANSWER.` · then, large: `WHERE WERE YOU.`

segments.voice: Find something wild to look at, a tree, a bird, the sky through a window; if not, a houseplant, or your own breath, which goes on without your permission. Let it be bigger than your questions for now, and notice that it doesn't need you to run it. If a question about your own life comes up, let it sit alongside the wild thing, not on top of it.
The whirlwind: out of the storm God answers Job with stars, sea and wild animals, a long run of questions, and not with a reason. Today's word.
Your line: where were you. The answer came as a world, not a reason. Day seven hundred twelve.

howItsDone: Jews and Christians read God's speeches from the whirlwind in Job 38–41 as scripture, and interpret them differently: as rebuke, as comfort, or as a widening of Job's view.

what a scholar hears: the speeches of Job 38–39 never mention the heavenly scenes of chapters 1–2, and Job's reply turns on hearing and seeing: 'now mine eye seeth thee' (Job 42:5).

chat.says: When God finally answers Job, does he explain why Job suffered?
options: No; he answers with questions about stars, sea and wild animals, not a reason.
Yes; he tells Job all about the test proposed in heaven in chapter one.
Yes; he says Job's friends were right and the suffering was earned.
chat.meaning: Out of the whirlwind God asks, "Where wast thou?" and shows Job the world. He never mentions chapter one's scene; Job is never told why.

notes: Editor: stock 'here's what's missing' reworded; 'ends the argument by showing Job the sky' changed to 'the world', since the speeches run on through animals (and chapters 40–41) rather than ending on the sky.

Paraphrased: Job 38:8–10 (who shut up the sea), 38:31 (Pleiades and Orion), 39:5–8 (wild ass scorns the multitude of the city), 39:9–12 (unicorn in the KJV, often rendered wild ox), 39:13–18 (ostrich; the KJV renders the bird differently in places). A Keeper should confirm the animal names used.
Hook: chapter after chapter of preparation refers to Job's speeches in Job 3–31.
Original: סְעָרָה as the word in Job 38:1 (מִן הַסְּעָרָה); confirm pointing and pronunciation.
The three readings of the speeches (rebuke, comfort, invitation) are attributed to readers and not ranked.
